name: Scalability Trilemma
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Pick Two: Why No Blockchain Does It All
lesson.summary: Vitalik Buterin's scalability trilemma holds that a blockchain can strongly optimize for at most two of three properties at once, decentralization, security, and scalability, and pushing too hard on one tends to erode one of the others.
lesson.body:
Ask a blockchain engineer to make a network faster, and the first question back should be: faster at the cost of what? The scalability trilemma, a framework popularized by Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin, holds that a blockchain can strongly optimize for at most two of three properties at once: decentralization (many ordinary participants can run a full node and meaningfully validate the chain), security (the network resists attacks, including a single actor or cartel rewriting history), and scalability (the network processes a high volume of transactions cheaply and quickly). Building on the definitions of scalability, decentralized trust, and the security attribute covered earlier, the trilemma describes tradeoffs among those three properties, not a law of physics, but it has proven a durable diagnostic tool.

The tension is easiest to see through the most naive scaling fix: make blocks bigger and let more transactions through. A bigger block raises throughput, but it also raises the computing power, bandwidth, and storage a node needs to keep up and store the growing chain history. Push block size high enough and only well-funded data centers can afford full validating nodes; everyone else is pushed toward trusting someone else's node, converting decentralized trust back into the institutional trust blockchains were built to avoid. This unfolded in Bitcoin's block size debate: raising the 1 megabyte limit promised more throughput, but critics warned it would concentrate node operation among fewer, larger operators, weakening resistance to capture.

Scaling can also be purchased by spending down security instead of decentralization. A chain that shrinks its validator set, or lets a small committee finalize blocks without the full network checking their work, processes transactions faster since fewer parties need to agree, but a smaller, faster-agreeing validator set is also a smaller set of parties who would need to collude to falsify the ledger. Early, poorly designed sharding proposals ran into a related problem: splitting a blockchain into shards that validate transactions independently increases throughput, but if each shard is secured by only a fraction of the validator pool, an attacker no longer needs the whole network, just one shard, making the chain easier to attack even though its aggregate hashpower looks unchanged.

The unresolved argument over Bitcoin's block size eventually became a governance crisis, not just a technical one: after years of debate on mailing lists and forums, the disagreement split the community, and a group of miners and developers launched Bitcoin Cash in 2017 with a larger block size, permanently forking away from Bitcoin's chain. That split previews a theme the rest of this chapter develops: tradeoffs like the trilemma do not resolve themselves, and how a blockchain decides who resolves them is its governance.

Modern designs try to escape the trilemma rather than pick a corner of it. Layer 2 rollups execute transactions off the main chain in batches, then post a compressed proof back to the base layer, which still checks the batch was valid, so throughput rises while security stays anchored to the decentralized base layer, the logic behind Ethereum's rollup-centric roadmap. Data availability sampling, used in proposals like Ethereum's danksharding, lets light nodes verify block data was published without downloading all of it. These approaches do not repeal the trilemma so much as move where the tradeoff bites, an exercise in the architecture tradeoff analysis covered later in this chapter.
